nodes.name: Três Corações

nodes.name: Bauru
nodes.headline: A city in the interior of São Paulo state where Pelé grew up and learned the game.

nodes.name: Santos
nodes.headline: The port city in São Paulo state that is home to Santos FC, Pelé's club for 18 years, and where he is buried.

nodes.name: São Paulo
nodes.headline: Brazil's largest city, where Pelé died at the Albert Einstein Israelite Hospital in December 2022.

nodes.name: Rio de Janeiro

nodes.name: Santo André

nodes.name: Maracanã Stadium
nodes.headline: Rio de Janeiro's great stadium, scene of Pelé's Brazil debut, the gol de placa, the 1,000th goal and his Brazil farewell.

nodes.name: Vila Belmiro (Estádio Urbano Caldeira)
nodes.headline: Santos FC's home ground, where Pelé played his last official match for the club in 1974 and lay in state in 2023.

nodes.name: Gothenburg

nodes.name: Ullevi
nodes.headline: Gothenburg stadium built for the 1958 World Cup; Pelé's first World Cup match and first World Cup goal came here.

nodes.name: Solna
nodes.headline: Municipality in the Stockholm area, home of the Råsunda Stadium.

nodes.name: Råsunda Stadium
nodes.headline: Sweden's former national stadium, where Brazil beat France and then Sweden in the 1958 semi-final and final.

nodes.name: Chile

nodes.name: Viña del Mar
nodes.headline: Chilean coastal city where Brazil played its 1962 World Cup group matches.

nodes.name: Sausalito Stadium
nodes.headline: Viña del Mar stadium where Pelé scored against Mexico and was injured against Czechoslovakia in 1962.

nodes.headline: Everton's long-time ground in Liverpool, where Brazil played Bulgaria, Hungary and Portugal in 1966.

nodes.headline: Mexican city where Brazil played five of its six matches at the 1970 World Cup.

nodes.name: Estadio Jalisco
nodes.headline: Guadalajara stadium where Brazil played its 1970 group games, quarter-final and semi-final.

nodes.name: Mexico City
nodes.headline: Mexico's capital, where the 1970 World Cup final was played.

nodes.headline: Mexico City stadium where Brazil beat Italy 4–1 in the 1970 World Cup final in front of 107,412 people.

nodes.name: Lisbon

nodes.name: Italy

nodes.name: United States
nodes.headline: Where Pelé played his last three seasons, for the New York Cosmos from 1975 to 1977.

nodes.name: Canada
nodes.headline: Home to several clubs of the North American Soccer League in Pelé's time.

nodes.name: New York City
nodes.headline: Home of the New York Cosmos, the club Pelé joined in June 1975.

nodes.name: Downing Stadium
nodes.headline: A stadium on Randalls Island in New York City, since demolished, where Pelé made his Cosmos debut in 1975.

nodes.name: East Rutherford
nodes.headline: New Jersey town in the Meadowlands, home of Giants Stadium.

nodes.name: Giants Stadium
nodes.headline: The Cosmos' home from 1977 and the scene of Pelé's farewell match on 1 October 1977.

nodes.name: Portland, Oregon
nodes.headline: Host city of Soccer Bowl '77, the last competitive match of Pelé's career.

nodes.name: Civic Stadium, Portland
nodes.headline: Portland stadium, now Providence Park, where the Cosmos won Soccer Bowl '77.

nodes.name: Nigeria
nodes.headline: Where Santos toured in 1969 during the civil war, the setting of a much-repeated but disputed ceasefire story.

nodes.name: Lagos
nodes.headline: Nigerian city where Santos drew 2–2 with Stationery Stores in 1969, the match linked to the ceasefire story.

nodes.name: Santos FC
nodes.headline: The São Paulo state club Pelé played for from 1956 to 1974, and for which he scored 643 goals in official matches.
nodes.story:
Santos Futebol Clube was founded in 1912 in the port city of Santos. It was already a two-time state champion when a 15-year-old Pelé arrived for a trial in 1956, brought by his youth coach Waldemar de Brito. He signed that June and stayed for 18 seasons.

With Pelé, Coutinho, Pepe, Zito and Dorval, Santos became one of the most admired teams in the world. The side is remembered in Brazil as *Os Santásticos*. It won ten Campeonato Paulista titles, six national championships, two Copa Libertadores (1962 and 1963) and two Intercontinental Cups (1962 and 1963) with him.

Because Pelé drew crowds everywhere, the club toured Europe, Africa, Asia and the Americas for lucrative friendlies. That is why his goal counts vary so much. English Wikipedia, working from RSSSF data, credits him with 643 goals in 659 official competitive matches for Santos. Counts that include friendlies are far higher, at about 1,091 goals.

He played his last official match for the club at Vila Belmiro on 2 October 1974. Santos was also where he was mourned: his coffin lay in state at Vila Belmiro in January 2023.

nodes.name: New York Cosmos
nodes.headline: The North American Soccer League club Pelé joined in 1975, winning the 1977 title in the last season of his career.
nodes.story:
The New York Cosmos were founded in 1970 and played in the North American Soccer League (NASL) from 1971 to 1984. Backed by Warner Communications, they spent years trying to sign Pelé. He agreed in June 1975, at the age of 34, after he had retired from Santos.

His arrival changed the club and the league. His first match, against the Dallas Tornado, was broadcast to 22 countries. Other stars followed him to the club, including Giorgio Chinaglia, Franz Beckenbauer and his old Brazil captain Carlos Alberto.

In 1977 the Cosmos moved to Giants Stadium in New Jersey, where crowds grew past 70,000. That season they won Soccer Bowl '77 against the Seattle Sounders, the last competitive match of Pelé's career. He said goodbye in an exhibition against Santos on 1 October 1977, and the club retired his number 10.

Counting NASL regular-season and play-off matches, Wikipedia credits him with 37 goals in 64 games. Including friendlies and tours, the figure is 66 goals in 107 games.

nodes.name: Brazil
nodes.headline: Brazil's national football team, for which Pelé won three World Cups and scored 77 goals in 92 matches between 1957 and 1971.
nodes.story:
Pelé first played for Brazil on 7 July 1957, aged 16, and scored in a 2–1 defeat by Argentina. He remains the youngest player to score for his country. His last match was a 2–2 draw with Yugoslavia at the Maracanã on 18 July 1971.

In between he played in four World Cups and won three of them, in 1958, 1962 and 1970. No other man has won three. He scored 12 goals in 14 World Cup matches.

His international totals depend on who is counting. Wikipedia's figure of 77 goals in 92 matches includes one 1968 match against a Rest of the World side that FIFA does not recognise as official. The Brazilian Football Confederation credits him with 95 goals in 113 matches, because it also counts games against club sides.

His 77 goals stood as Brazil's record for more than fifty years, until Neymar passed it in September 2023. With Pelé on the pitch, Brazil won 67, drew 14 and lost 11. Brazil never lost a match in which both Pelé and Garrincha played.

nodes.name: Bauru Atlético Clube
nodes.headline: The club in Bauru whose junior team Pelé played for as a boy, coached by Waldemar de Brito.
nodes.story: Bauru Atlético Clube was a football club in Bauru, in the interior of São Paulo state. Pelé played for its junior side as a teenager, under the coaching of the former Brazil forward Waldemar de Brito. Wikipedia records that he led the juniors to two São Paulo state youth titles. It was de Brito who took him to Santos for a trial in 1956.

nodes.name: Corinthians de Santo André
nodes.headline: The club Santos beat 7–1 in a friendly on 7 September 1956, the day a 15-year-old Pelé scored his first senior goal.
nodes.story: Corinthians Futebol Clube, from Santo André in Greater São Paulo, were Santos's opponents in a friendly on 7 September 1956. Pelé scored, his first goal as a senior player, in a 7–1 win. Their goalkeeper, Zaluar, was later known as the man who conceded Pelé's first goal.

nodes.name: Argentina
nodes.headline: Brazil's neighbours and rivals, against whom a 16-year-old Pelé made his international debut and scored in 1957.
nodes.story: Argentina beat Brazil 2–1 at the Maracanã on 7 July 1957 in the Roca Cup, the match in which Pelé first played and scored for his country. Two years later Argentina won the 1959 South American Championship on home soil, with Brazil second and Pelé the top scorer.

nodes.name: Soviet Union
nodes.headline: Brazil's opponents in Pelé's first World Cup match, a 2–0 win in Gothenburg on 15 June 1958.
nodes.story: The Soviet Union were the 1956 Olympic champions and were playing their first World Cup in 1958. Brazil met them in the last group match in Gothenburg. Pelé and Garrincha played their first World Cup games that day, and Brazil won 2–0 with two goals from Vavá.

nodes.name: Wales
nodes.headline: The team Pelé scored his first World Cup goal against, in Brazil's 1–0 quarter-final win in 1958.
nodes.story:
Wales reached the 1958 quarter-finals after drawing all three group games and beating Hungary in a play-off. They held Brazil until the 66th minute in Gothenburg, when Pelé scored the only goal of the match.

The match was played at Ullevi in Gothenburg before 25,923 people.

nodes.name: France
nodes.headline: Brazil's semi-final opponents in 1958, beaten 5–2 as Pelé scored a second-half hat-trick.
nodes.story:
France came to the 1958 semi-final with Just Fontaine, who scored a record 13 goals at that tournament. The score was 2–1 to Brazil at half-time. In the second half Pelé scored three times, and Brazil won 5–2.

France went on to beat West Germany 6–3 for third place, with Fontaine scoring four.

nodes.name: Sweden
nodes.headline: The hosts of the 1958 World Cup, beaten 5–2 by Brazil in the final, in which Pelé scored twice.
nodes.story: Sweden reached the 1958 final on home soil and took the lead after four minutes through Nils Liedholm. Brazil replied with five goals, two of them from Pelé, and won 5–2. Sweden remains the only host nation to lose a World Cup final.

nodes.name: Fluminense
nodes.headline: Rio de Janeiro club beaten 3–1 by Santos at the Maracanã in March 1961, the match of Pelé's gol de placa.
nodes.story: Fluminense Football Club is one of Rio de Janeiro's major clubs. On 5 March 1961, in the Torneio Rio–São Paulo, they lost 3–1 to Santos at the Maracanã. Pelé's solo goal that night, past goalkeeper Castilho, became known as the gol de placa.

nodes.name: Mexico
nodes.headline: Brazil's first opponents at the 1962 World Cup, beaten 2–0 with a goal from Pelé.
nodes.story: Mexico met Brazil in Viña del Mar on 30 May 1962. Pelé set up Zagallo for the first goal and scored the second in a 2–0 win. It was his only goal of that tournament. Eight years later Mexico hosted the World Cup that Brazil won.

nodes.name: Czechoslovakia
nodes.headline: Opponents in two of Pelé's World Cups: he was injured against them in 1962 and scored against them in 1970.
nodes.story: Czechoslovakia drew 0–0 with Brazil in 1962, the match in which Pelé was injured and lost for the tournament. They met Brazil again in the 1962 final and lost 3–1. In 1970 they opened Brazil's tournament in Guadalajara; Brazil won 4–1, Pelé scored, and he nearly scored from his own half against goalkeeper Ivo Viktor.

nodes.name: Benfica
nodes.headline: The Lisbon club Santos beat for the 1962 Intercontinental Cup, with Pelé scoring five goals over the two legs.
nodes.story: Sport Lisboa e Benfica were European champions in 1961 and 1962, with Eusébio in attack. In the 1962 Intercontinental Cup, Santos won 3–2 in Rio and 5–2 in Lisbon. Pelé scored twice in the first leg and three times in the second.

nodes.name: Bulgaria
nodes.headline: Brazil's first opponents at the 1966 World Cup: Pelé scored, but was fouled repeatedly and missed the next match.
nodes.story:
Bulgaria lost 2–0 to Brazil at Goodison Park on 12 July 1966. Pelé scored the first goal and Garrincha the second. The Bulgarian defenders fouled Pelé throughout, and he was not fit for the next game.

Bulgaria lost all three of their group matches.

nodes.name: Portugal
nodes.headline: The team that knocked Brazil out of the 1966 World Cup with a 3–1 win, as Pelé was fouled out of the match.
nodes.story:
Portugal, led by Eusébio, beat Brazil 3–1 at Goodison Park on 19 July 1966. The defender João Morais fouled Pelé twice without being sent off. Portugal went on to finish third.

Portugal went on to finish third, their best World Cup result to that point.

nodes.name: Vasco da Gama
nodes.headline: The Rio de Janeiro club Pelé scored his 1,000th goal against, from a penalty at the Maracanã in November 1969.
nodes.story: Club de Regatas Vasco da Gama is one of Rio de Janeiro's big clubs. On 19 November 1969 they lost 2–1 to Santos at the Maracanã. Pelé's winning penalty, past the Argentine goalkeeper Edgardo Andrada, was counted as his 1,000th goal.

nodes.name: England
nodes.headline: The 1966 world champions, beaten 1–0 by Brazil in 1970 in the match of Gordon Banks's save from Pelé.
nodes.story: England arrived in Mexico in 1970 as world champions. Their group match with Brazil in Guadalajara on 7 June was the most anticipated of the first round. Gordon Banks stopped a Pelé header, and Jairzinho scored the only goal in the second half.

nodes.name: Uruguay
nodes.headline: Brazil's semi-final opponents at the 1970 World Cup, beaten 3–1 in Guadalajara.
nodes.story: Uruguay had beaten Brazil in the deciding match of the 1950 World Cup at the Maracanã. In the 1970 semi-final they scored first, but Brazil won 3–1. Pelé did not score, but his dummy on goalkeeper Ladislao Mazurkiewicz became one of the best-known moments of the tournament.

nodes.name: Italy
nodes.headline: Brazil's opponents in the 1970 World Cup final, beaten 4–1 at the Estadio Azteca.
nodes.story: Italy and Brazil had both won the World Cup twice before 1970, so the winner of the final would keep the Jules Rimet Trophy. Pelé headed Brazil in front, Roberto Boninsegna equalised, and Brazil scored three more in the second half.

nodes.name: Yugoslavia
nodes.headline: The opponents in Pelé's last match for Brazil, a 2–2 draw at the Maracanã on 18 July 1971.
nodes.story:
Yugoslavia drew 2–2 with Brazil at the Maracanã on 18 July 1971, in Pelé's farewell from the national team. Rivellino and Gérson scored for Brazil.

The match was a friendly arranged as Pelé's goodbye to the national team, and it drew a very large crowd to the Maracanã.

nodes.name: Ponte Preta
nodes.headline: The Campinas club Santos beat 2–0 at Vila Belmiro on 2 October 1974, Pelé's last official match for Santos.
nodes.story: Associação Atlética Ponte Preta, from Campinas in São Paulo state, were Santos's opponents in the Campeonato Paulista on 2 October 1974. Santos won 2–0, and Pelé left the field during the first half, kneeling to salute the crowd, in his last official game for the club.

nodes.name: Dallas Tornado
nodes.headline: The NASL club the Cosmos drew 2–2 with on 15 June 1975, Pelé's first match for New York.
nodes.story:
The Dallas Tornado played in the North American Soccer League from 1968 to 1981. They were the Cosmos' opponents in an exhibition at Downing Stadium on 15 June 1975, Pelé's first game for the club, which ended 2–2.

The match drew 22,278 people and more than 300 journalists.

nodes.name: Seattle Sounders
nodes.headline: The NASL club the Cosmos beat 2–1 in Soccer Bowl '77, the last competitive match of Pelé's career.
nodes.story:
The Seattle Sounders played in the NASL from 1974 to 1983. They reached Soccer Bowl '77 in Portland, Oregon, and lost 2–1 to the Cosmos on 28 August 1977.

Steve Hunt and Giorgio Chinaglia scored for the Cosmos, and Tommy Ord for Seattle. The crowd was 35,548.

nodes.name: FIFA World Cup 1958
nodes.headline: Brazil's first World Cup title, won in Sweden, where a 17-year-old Pelé scored six goals in four matches.
nodes.story:
The sixth World Cup was played in Sweden from 8 to 29 June 1958. Brazil, coached by Vicente Feola, had never won the tournament.

Pelé arrived with a knee injury and missed the first two matches, a 3–0 win over Austria and a 0–0 draw with England. He came into the side for the last group game, against the Soviet Union, alongside Garrincha. Brazil won 2–0.

In the quarter-final against Wales he scored the only goal, at 17 years and 239 days, then the youngest scorer in World Cup history. In the semi-final he scored three second-half goals as Brazil beat France 5–2. In the final he scored twice more in a 5–2 win over the hosts.

He finished with six goals in four matches and was named the tournament's best young player. Brazil became the first team to win a World Cup outside its own continent. After Sweden, the Brazilian press began calling him *O Rei*, the King.

The tournament also made Garrincha and Didi famous, and Didi was named its best player. Just Fontaine of France scored 13 goals, still a record for one World Cup. The 1958 final remains the highest-scoring World Cup final, and Sweden the only host nation to lose one.

nodes.name: South American Championship 1959 (Argentina)
nodes.headline: The continental championship held in Buenos Aires in 1959, where Pelé was top scorer with eight goals and named best player.
nodes.story:
The 1959 South American Championship, the forerunner of the Copa América, was played in Buenos Aires from 7 March to 4 April. Seven teams played each other once.

Brazil went through the tournament unbeaten but finished second to Argentina on points. Pelé, then 18, scored eight goals in six matches, including a hat-trick against Paraguay. He was the tournament's top scorer and was named its best player.

It was his only appearance in the competition. (Wikipedia's list of his international goals gives the figure as six appearances and eight goals in its table, although its introduction states the numbers differently.)

All the matches were played at the Estadio Monumental in Buenos Aires. Colombia and Ecuador withdrew, leaving Argentina, Brazil, Paraguay, Peru, Uruguay, Chile and Bolivia. A second South American Championship was held in Ecuador later the same year.

His eight goals came in five of Brazil's six matches. He was 18, had already won a World Cup, and was scoring prolifically for Santos at the same time.

Brazil drew 2–2 with Peru, beat Chile 3–0, Bolivia 4–2, Uruguay 3–1 and Paraguay 4–1, and drew 1–1 with Argentina in the last match. Pelé scored in every game except the win over Uruguay. A win over Argentina would have given Brazil the title; Pelé's equaliser was not enough.

nodes.name: FIFA World Cup 1962
nodes.headline: Brazil's second World Cup title, won in Chile after Pelé was injured in the second match.
nodes.story:
The seventh World Cup was played in Chile from 30 May to 17 June 1962. Pelé, now 21, was widely seen as the best player in the world.

In Brazil's first match, against Mexico in Viña del Mar, he set up the first goal for Zagallo and scored the second himself in a 2–0 win. In the second match, against Czechoslovakia, he was hurt while trying a long-range shot. Substitutes were not allowed, so he stayed on, and the game ended 0–0. He did not play again in the tournament.

Garrincha led the team in his absence, and Amarildo came into the side. Brazil beat Czechoslovakia 3–1 in the final in Santiago.

At the time only players who appeared in the final received medals. FIFA changed the rule in 1978, and Pelé was given his 1962 winner's medal in 2007.

Garrincha was named the tournament's best player and shared the top scorer's prize with five others, including Vavá. Brazil became the second country, after Italy, to win two World Cups in a row.

Brazil's path was Mexico (2–0), Czechoslovakia (0–0) and Spain (2–1) in the group, then England (3–1) in the quarter-final, Chile (4–2) in the semi-final and Czechoslovakia again in the final, watched by 68,679 people at the Estadio Nacional.

nodes.name: Copa Libertadores 1962
nodes.headline: Santos's first South American club title, won against Peñarol with two Pelé goals in the deciding match.
nodes.story:
Santos qualified for the third Copa Libertadores by winning the 1961 Taça Brasil. They won their first-round group and beat Universidad Católica in the semi-finals.

The final against the holders, Peñarol of Uruguay, went to three matches. Santos won 2–1 in Montevideo and lost 3–2 in Santos, so a play-off was held at the Estadio Monumental in Buenos Aires on 30 August 1962. Santos won 3–0, and Pelé scored twice.

He scored four goals in the competition. It was the first time a Brazilian club had won the Libertadores.

Only 51 minutes of the second leg were counted as official by CONMEBOL; Santos scored again in the unofficial time that followed, but the result stood as a 3–2 defeat. The play-off was refereed by the Dutchman Leo Horn.

Winning the Libertadores took Santos into the Intercontinental Cup against Benfica that autumn, and that same year they also won the Campeonato Paulista and the Taça Brasil.

In the group stage Santos won every match but one, a 1–1 draw away to Cerro Porteño. In the home game against Cerro at Vila Belmiro they won 9–1, with two goals from Pelé and three from Coutinho. Peñarol's Alberto Spencer scored three of their four goals in the final.

nodes.name: Intercontinental Cup 1962
nodes.headline: Santos's first world club title, won against Benfica in 1962; Pelé scored five goals in the two legs.
nodes.story:
The Intercontinental Cup matched the champions of Europe and South America. In 1962 it was Benfica, with Eusébio, against Santos, with Pelé.

In the first leg at the Maracanã on 19 September, Santos won 3–2 and Pelé scored twice. In the second leg in Lisbon on 11 October, in front of 73,000 people, he scored a hat-trick in a 5–2 win.

Wikipedia describes the Lisbon match as the finest performance ever seen in the competition. Benfica's goalkeeper, Costa Pereira, is quoted there as saying he had come hoping to stop a great man but left feeling beaten by someone not born on the same planet.

The first leg drew 85,459 people to the Maracanã. Benfica's two goals in Rio came from Santana; in Lisbon, Eusébio and Santana scored only after Santos led 5–0. Pelé's seven goals across 1962 and 1963 make him the competition's all-time top scorer, and he is the only player to score a hat-trick in it.

In the first leg Pelé scored in the 31st and 85th minutes and Coutinho in the 64th. Santos were coached by Lula, and their side included Gilmar, Zito, Coutinho and Pepe as well as Pelé. The Paraguayan Rubén Cabrera refereed the first leg and the Frenchman Pierre Schwinte the second.

nodes.name: Copa Libertadores 1963
nodes.headline: Santos's second straight South American title, won against Boca Juniors; Pelé scored the winner in Buenos Aires.
nodes.story:
As holders, Santos went straight into the semi-finals of the 1963 Copa Libertadores. There they beat Botafogo, whose team included Garrincha and Jairzinho.

In the final against Boca Juniors, Santos won 3–2 at the Maracanã on 3 September. In the second leg at Boca's ground in Buenos Aires on 11 September, Coutinho equalised and Pelé scored the winner eight minutes from time for a 2–1 win.

Pelé scored five goals in the tournament, joint second behind Boca's José Sanfilippo.

The first leg at the Maracanã drew 100,000 people. Coutinho scored twice and Lima added a third, before Sanfilippo's late goal made it 3–2. Santos had won the competition twice in its first four years, both times with Pelé.

It was part of a busy year in which Santos also won the Torneio Rio–São Paulo, the Taça Brasil and, later, the Intercontinental Cup.

The second leg drew 50,000 people to Boca's stadium. Sanfilippo put Boca ahead just after half-time, Coutinho equalised, and Pelé scored the winner in the 82nd minute. The final was decided on points: two wins gave Santos four points to Boca's none. The French referee Marcel Bois took charge of both legs. Pelé was 22 at the time.

nodes.name: Intercontinental Cup 1963
nodes.headline: Santos's second world club title, won against AC Milan after a play-off in Rio, with Pelé playing only the first leg.
nodes.story:
In 1963 Santos met AC Milan, the European champions. In the first leg at the San Siro on 16 October, Milan won 4–2. Pelé scored both Santos goals, the second from a penalty.

He did not play in the return leg or the play-off. Santos won the second leg 4–2 at the Maracanã, and because the competition was decided on points, a play-off was held two days later at the same stadium. Santos won it 1–0 with a penalty from Dalmo.

Both Rio matches were controversial. Milan complained about the refereeing of the Argentine official Juan Brozzi, and Milan's captain Cesare Maldini was sent off in the play-off.

The second leg at the Maracanã drew 132,728 people and the play-off 120,421. Santos's winner in the play-off came from a penalty that many reporters considered a dive. Even so, Santos became the first club to win the Intercontinental Cup twice in a row.

Pelé captained Santos in the first leg, in which Giovanni Trapattoni, Amarildo (twice) and Bruno Mora scored for Milan. In the second leg Milan led 2–0 at half-time; Santos scored four in the second half, three of them from free kicks. The referee, Brozzi, was later expelled by his own federation.

nodes.name: FIFA World Cup 1966
nodes.headline: The World Cup in England where Brazil, the holders, went out in the first round as Pelé was fouled out of two matches.
nodes.story:
The eighth World Cup was played in England from 11 to 30 July 1966. Brazil were the holders, with Vicente Feola back as coach, and were expected to do well.

In the first match, against Bulgaria at Goodison Park, Pelé scored the opening goal. That made him the first player to score at three successive World Cups. But he was fouled again and again, and was not fit to play the next match. Brazil lost it 3–1 to Hungary.

He returned, not fully fit, for the last group game against Portugal. The defender João Morais fouled him twice and was not sent off, a decision often listed among the worst refereeing errors in World Cup history. Accounts differ on whether Pelé limped on to the end or was carried off. Brazil lost 3–1 and went out.

Afterwards Pelé said he would not play at a World Cup again. He changed his mind in 1969.

England won the tournament, beating West Germany in the final at Wembley.

Against Hungary, without Pelé, Tostão scored Brazil's goal, but Ferenc Bene, János Farkas and Kálmán Mészöly scored for Hungary in front of 51,387 people. The Hungary match was refereed by Ken Dagnall of England. Portugal and Hungary went through from the group.

nodes.name: FIFA World Cup 1970
nodes.headline: Brazil's third World Cup title, won in Mexico by a team often called the best ever; it was Pelé's last World Cup.
nodes.story:
The ninth World Cup was played in Mexico from 31 May to 21 June 1970. Pelé was 29. He had first refused to rejoin the national team in 1969, then agreed, and scored six goals in six qualifiers.

Coached by Mário Zagallo, Brazil played an attacking side with Jairzinho, Gérson, Tostão, Rivellino and Pelé. They won all six matches. Pelé scored against Czechoslovakia and twice against Romania in the group stage. Between those games came the 1–0 win over England, in which Gordon Banks made his save from Pelé's header.

Brazil beat Peru 4–2 in the quarter-final and Uruguay 3–1 in the semi-final. In the final against Italy at the Estadio Azteca, Pelé headed the first goal and set up two more in a 4–1 win.

He finished with four goals and is credited with six assists. FIFA later named him the tournament's best player, awarding him the Golden Ball retrospectively. Brazil's third title let them keep the Jules Rimet Trophy, and Pelé became the only player to win three World Cups.

It was the first World Cup broadcast live around the world, and in a few places in colour, so this Brazil team was seen by more people than any before it. Brazil's 1970 team is often called the greatest in history. Jairzinho scored in every match, Carlos Alberto captained the side, and Zagallo became the first man to win the World Cup as player and coach.

nodes.name: North American Soccer League 1977
nodes.headline: Pelé's last season as a professional, which ended with the New York Cosmos winning Soccer Bowl '77.
nodes.story:
The 1977 NASL season was Pelé's third and last with the New York Cosmos. The team moved that year to the new Giants Stadium in New Jersey and briefly called itself simply "Cosmos".

Pelé, aged 36 and 37 during the season, scored 13 goals in 25 regular-season matches and four in six play-off games, by Wikipedia's count. In June he scored a hat-trick in a 3–0 win over the Tampa Bay Rowdies. A play-off match against the Fort Lauderdale Strikers drew a record crowd for American soccer, and the Cosmos won it 8–3.

The Cosmos beat the Rochester Lancers in the semi-finals and the Seattle Sounders 2–1 in Soccer Bowl '77 in Portland, Oregon, on 28 August. It was the last competitive match of his career.

The Cosmos had signed Franz Beckenbauer and Carlos Alberto that year, and the coach Gordon Bradley was replaced by Eddie Firmani midway through. Pelé was named to the league's all-star team for the third year running.

The championship was the Cosmos' second North American title. His last match of all, an exhibition against Santos, came five weeks after the final.

In the regular season the Cosmos finished second in their four-team division and third of 18 teams overall. In the play-offs they beat Rochester 4–1 in the second leg of the semi-final.

nodes.name: Santos 7–1 Corinthians de Santo André
nodes.headline: Pelé's first match for Santos, aged 15, in which he scored the first goal of his senior career.
nodes.story:
On 7 September 1956, Brazil's Independence Day, Santos played a friendly against Corinthians de Santo André in Santo André. Pelé was 15 and had signed for the club that June.

Santos won 7–1, and Pelé scored one of the goals. It was the first goal of his senior career. The opposing goalkeeper, Zaluar, later described himself on his business card as the man who let in Pelé's first goal.

The next season Pelé was a regular in the Santos team, and at 16 he was the top scorer in the Campeonato Paulista.

Santos were the reigning state champions, having won the Campeonato Paulista in 1955 and 1956. Pelé had joined them after a trial at Vila Belmiro, where he impressed the coach, Lula. The match itself was a minor friendly, but it is remembered as the start of a career that lasted more than twenty years.

nodes.name: Brazil 1–2 Argentina
nodes.headline: Pelé's first match for Brazil, at 16, in which he scored and became his country's youngest goalscorer.
nodes.story:
Ten months after turning professional, Pelé was called up by Brazil for the Roca Cup, a two-match series against Argentina. The first match was played at the Maracanã on 7 July 1957.

Argentina won 2–1, but Pelé scored Brazil's goal. He was 16 years and 259 days old. He is still the youngest player to score for Brazil.

Three days later, at the Pacaembu in São Paulo, he scored again as Brazil won the second match 2–0 after extra time and took the trophy.

At 16 years and 259 days he was also the youngest player ever to appear for Brazil. Less than a year later he was in the squad for the World Cup in Sweden.

It was the first of his 92 matches for Brazil.

nodes.name: Brazil 2–0 Soviet Union
nodes.headline: Pelé's first World Cup match, aged 17, in which Brazil beat the Soviet Union with two goals from Vavá.
nodes.story:
Brazil had beaten Austria and drawn with England without Pelé, who had a knee injury. For the third group match, at Ullevi in Gothenburg, coach Vicente Feola picked him and Garrincha.

A team psychologist had advised against playing the 17-year-old. Feola played him anyway. Garrincha's dribbling troubled the Soviet defence from the start, and Vavá scored twice. Pelé did not score but set up Vavá's second goal.

Brazil won 2–0 and topped the group. The crowd was 50,928.

Brazil finished first in their group without conceding a goal. The Soviet Union, the 1956 Olympic champions, also went through after beating England in a play-off. The referee was Maurice Guigue of France, who also took charge of the final.

Garrincha, too, was making his World Cup debut.

nodes.name: Brazil 1–0 Wales
nodes.headline: The quarter-final in which Pelé scored his first World Cup goal, the only goal of the match, at 17.
nodes.story:
Wales had reached the quarter-finals of their only World Cup of the century by drawing all three group games and beating Hungary in a play-off. In Gothenburg they held Brazil for 66 minutes.

Then Pelé scored. At 17 years and 239 days, he became the youngest scorer in World Cup history at the time. It was the only goal of the game, and it took Brazil into the semi-finals.

The crowd at Ullevi was 25,923.

Brazil went on to meet France in the semi-final five days later. The referee was the Austrian Fritz Seipelt.

Brazil had needed most of the match to break Wales down. It was the first of three knockout games in a row in which Pelé scored, a run that continued against France in the semi-final and Sweden in the final.

nodes.name: Brazil 5–2 France
nodes.headline: The 1958 semi-final in which Pelé scored a second-half hat-trick, the youngest player ever to do so at a World Cup.
nodes.story:
Brazil met France at the Råsunda Stadium in Solna. Vavá scored after two minutes and Just Fontaine equalised. Didi put Brazil 2–1 ahead before half-time. France lost their captain, Robert Jonquet, to a broken leg in the first half and played on with ten men, as substitutes were not allowed.

In the second half Pelé scored three times, in the 52nd, 64th and 75th minutes. Roger Piantoni pulled one back late on, and Brazil won 5–2.

Pelé was 17 years and 244 days old. He remains the youngest player to score a hat-trick at a World Cup. The crowd was 27,100.

Fontaine's goal was one of the 13 he scored at that tournament, still the record for a single World Cup. The Welsh referee was Benjamin Griffiths. The win took Brazil into their first World Cup final; in 1950, on home soil, the title had been decided in a final group, not a final.

nodes.name: Brazil 5–2 Sweden
nodes.headline: The 1958 World Cup final, Brazil's first title, in which 17-year-old Pelé scored twice against the hosts.
nodes.story:
The final was played at the Råsunda Stadium on 29 June 1958 in front of 49,737 people. Sweden's captain Nils Liedholm scored after four minutes. Vavá equalised five minutes later and gave Brazil the lead before half-time.

Ten minutes into the second half Pelé controlled the ball in the penalty area, lifted it over a defender and volleyed it in. Zagallo made it 4–1. Agne Simonsson scored for Sweden, and in the last minute Pelé headed the fifth.

At 17 years and 249 days, Pelé became the youngest player to appear in, score in and win a World Cup final. At the final whistle he collapsed on the pitch, then wept on the shoulder of goalkeeper Gilmar.

It is still the highest-scoring World Cup final.

nodes.name: Santos 3–1 Fluminense
nodes.headline: The match at the Maracanã in which Pelé scored the solo goal that gave Brazil the phrase gol de placa.
nodes.story:
Santos played Fluminense at the Maracanã on 5 March 1961, in the Torneio Rio–São Paulo. Near the end of the first half, Pelé picked up the ball deep in his own half and ran the length of the field. He went past several defenders before beating goalkeeper Castilho.

The crowd, Fluminense supporters included, applauded for a long time. A commemorative plaque was later put up at the stadium for what it called the most beautiful goal in the Maracanã's history. That plaque gave Brazilian football the phrase *gol de placa*, a goal worthy of a plaque.

Santos won 3–1.

Pelé was 20 at the time. The goal was scored in Rio against a Rio club, which made the applause of the home crowd all the more striking. The phrase it inspired is still part of everyday Brazilian football talk, used for any goal worth commemorating.

nodes.name: Brazil 2–0 Mexico
nodes.headline: Brazil's first match of the 1962 World Cup, in which Pelé set up one goal and scored the other.
nodes.story:
Brazil began the defence of their title against Mexico at the Sausalito Stadium in Viña del Mar. The first half was goalless.

In the 56th minute Pelé set up Zagallo for the opening goal. In the 73rd he scored the second himself. It was his only goal of the tournament.

The crowd was 10,484.

Brazil were the holders and had kept much of their 1958 side. Their coach was now Aymoré Moreira. The other teams in the group were Czechoslovakia and Spain. Pelé would play only one more match at the tournament, three days later, before injury ended his part in it. Brazil went on to retain the title without him, beating Czechoslovakia 3–1 in the final in Santiago.

Pelé was 21.

nodes.name: Brazil 0–0 Czechoslovakia
nodes.headline: The 1962 group match in which Pelé was injured, ending his tournament; Brazil went on to win it without him.
nodes.story:
Brazil's second match in Chile was against Czechoslovakia in Viña del Mar. During the match Pelé hurt himself while trying a long-range shot.

Substitutes were not yet allowed, so he stayed on the pitch, unable to play a full part. The match finished 0–0.

He missed the rest of the tournament. Brazil met Czechoslovakia again in the final and won 3–1. The crowd in Viña del Mar was 14,903.

Brazil still had to beat Spain in their last group match. Amarildo, from Botafogo, came in for Pelé and scored both goals in a 2–1 win. Later, at a time when only players in the final received medals, Pelé went without one; FIFA presented him with a winner's medal for 1962 in 2007.

nodes.name: Santos 5–2 Benfica
nodes.headline: Santos's 5–2 win in Lisbon that won the 1962 Intercontinental Cup, with a Pelé hat-trick.
nodes.story:
Santos had won the first leg 3–2 in Rio. The return match was played at Benfica's Estádio da Luz in Lisbon on 11 October 1962, before 73,000 people.

Pelé scored in the 15th and 25th minutes, Coutinho added a third early in the second half, and Pelé completed his hat-trick in the 64th minute. Pepe made it 5–0 before Eusébio and Santana scored late for Benfica.

Santos became world club champions. The match is often described as one of the best performances of Pelé's career.

Benfica had won the European Cup in 1961 and 1962. The tie is remembered as a meeting of Pelé and Eusébio, the two leading forwards of the 1960s, who faced each other only three times. The French referee was Pierre Schwinte. Afterwards Benfica's goalkeeper, Costa Pereira, said he had felt beaten by someone not of this world.

nodes.name: Brazil 2–0 Bulgaria
nodes.headline: Brazil's first match at the 1966 World Cup, in which Pelé scored but was fouled so often he missed the next game.
nodes.story:
Brazil opened their 1966 campaign at Goodison Park in Liverpool. Pelé scored in the 15th minute and Garrincha added a second in the 63rd.

The goal made Pelé the first player to score at three World Cups in a row. But the Bulgarian defenders fouled him throughout, and he left with a knee injury that kept him out of the next match, a 3–1 defeat by Hungary.

The crowd was 47,308.

Brazil were two-time holders and had Vicente Feola back in charge. The rough treatment Pelé received in this match set the tone for the tournament, which is remembered for its physical play and inconsistent refereeing. Feola expected other teams to target him in the same way, and they did.

nodes.name: Brazil 1–3 Portugal
nodes.headline: The match that knocked Brazil out of the 1966 World Cup, remembered for the fouls on Pelé.
nodes.story:
Brazil needed to beat Portugal at Goodison Park to have a chance of reaching the quarter-finals. Pelé was brought back, though not fully fit.

António Simões and Eusébio put Portugal 2–0 up in the first half. The defender João Morais fouled Pelé twice, and the English referee George McCabe did not send him off. Pelé could barely run for the rest of the evening. Rildo pulled a goal back, and Eusébio scored again five minutes from time.

Brazil were out. Pelé said afterwards he would not play at another World Cup. The crowd was 58,479.

Portugal went on to finish third, and Eusébio was the tournament's top scorer with nine goals. It was the last time Pelé played at the tournament until Mexico, four years later.

nodes.name: Santos 2–1 Vasco da Gama
nodes.headline: The match at the Maracanã in which Pelé scored the penalty counted as his 1,000th goal.
nodes.story:
By November 1969 all of Brazil was waiting for Pelé's 1,000th goal, by the count kept at the time, which included friendlies. Santos played Vasco da Gama at the Maracanã on 19 November in the national championship, then called the Torneio Roberto Gomes Pedrosa.

Late in the second half, with the score 1–1, Santos were given a penalty. Pelé took it and beat the Argentine goalkeeper Edgardo Andrada, who got a hand to the ball. Fans ran onto the pitch, and the game was held up while he was carried around.

Santos won 2–1. Reported crowd figures vary widely, from about 65,000 to 80,000, and the minute of the goal is also given differently.

The goal became known as *O Milésimo*, "the thousandth". Pelé dedicated it to the children of Brazil, and the post office issued a commemorative stamp. Since the count included friendlies, the milestone is part of the long debate about how many goals he really scored.

nodes.name: Brazil 4–1 Czechoslovakia
nodes.headline: Brazil's first match of the 1970 World Cup, in which Pelé scored and almost scored from his own half.
nodes.story:
Brazil opened the 1970 World Cup at the Estadio Jalisco in Guadalajara. Ladislav Petráš put Czechoslovakia ahead in the 11th minute, and Rivellino equalised from a free kick.

In the 59th minute Pelé put Brazil ahead, becoming the second player after Uwe Seeler to score at four World Cups. Later in the game he saw the goalkeeper, Ivo Viktor, standing off his line and shot from inside his own half. The ball went just wide. Jairzinho scored twice more.

The crowd was 52,897.

It was Brazil's first match under Mário Zagallo at the finals and the first sign of how freely the new team would attack. The two sides had also met in the 1962 final, when Brazil won 3–1.

nodes.name: Brazil 1–0 England
nodes.headline: The 1970 group match between the holders and Brazil, remembered for Gordon Banks's save from Pelé's header.
nodes.story:
England were world champions, and this match in Guadalajara was the most awaited of the first round. It kicked off at noon, in front of 66,843 people.

Jairzinho crossed from the right and Pelé headed the ball down towards the corner. Gordon Banks dived across, got his hand to it as it bounced and turned it over the bar. It is often called the save of the century.

In the 59th minute Pelé laid the ball off to Jairzinho, who scored the only goal. At the end Pelé and the England captain Bobby Moore swapped shirts and embraced. The photograph of that moment is often used to show sportsmanship.

Banks had been told the day before that he would be made an OBE. The match did not decide the group, as both teams went through, but it was the meeting most people wanted to see. England went out in the quarter-finals to West Germany, with Banks unable to play because of illness.

nodes.name: Brazil 3–1 Uruguay
nodes.headline: The 1970 semi-final Brazil won 3–1, remembered for Pelé's dummy that left goalkeeper Mazurkiewicz stranded.
nodes.story:
The semi-final was moved from Mexico City to Guadalajara three days before it was played, despite Uruguay's protests. Luis Cubilla put Uruguay ahead in the 19th minute. Clodoaldo equalised just before half-time, and Jairzinho and Rivellino scored in the second half.

Pelé did not score, but he made one of the best-known plays of his career. Tostão sent him through, and goalkeeper Ladislao Mazurkiewicz came out. Pelé let the ball run past the keeper on one side while he ran round the other. He reached it and shot, but the ball went just wide of the far post.

The crowd was 51,261.

Uruguay had beaten Brazil at the Maracanã in the deciding match of the 1950 World Cup, and the semi-final was charged with that memory. Rivellino's goal in the last minute came from Pelé's pass. Mazurkiewicz was later named the best goalkeeper of the tournament.

nodes.name: Brazil 4–1 Italy
nodes.headline: The 1970 World Cup final, in which Pelé scored the first goal and set up two more as Brazil won a third title.
nodes.story:
The final was played at the Estadio Azteca in Mexico City on 21 June 1970, before 107,412 people. In the 18th minute Pelé, marked by Tarcisio Burgnich, headed in Rivellino's cross. It was Brazil's 100th goal at World Cups.

Roberto Boninsegna equalised after a defensive mistake. In the second half Gérson scored from long range. Pelé then headed a long free kick down for Jairzinho to make it 3–1.

The last goal is one of the most replayed in football. The move passed through most of the team, and Pelé, without looking, rolled the ball into the path of Carlos Alberto, who struck it in from the right. Brazil won 4–1, and Pelé became the first player to win three World Cups.

The referee was Rudi Glöckner of East Germany. Mário Zagallo became the first man to win the World Cup as a player and as a coach. Carlos Alberto's goal was later voted 36th in a British poll of the greatest sporting moments, and the Italian defender who marked Pelé, Tarcisio Burgnich, later said he had underestimated him.

nodes.name: Brazil 2–2 Yugoslavia
nodes.headline: Pelé's last match for Brazil, a friendly at the Maracanã that ended 2–2.
nodes.story:
Pelé chose to retire from international football in 1971, at 30. His last match was a friendly against Yugoslavia at the Maracanã on 18 July.

Rivellino and Gérson scored for Brazil, and Džajić and Jerković for Yugoslavia, in a 2–2 draw. Pelé did not score. His last international goal had come a week earlier, against Austria in São Paulo.

The crowd was very large, but reported figures differ, from about 138,000 to 180,000. He did not play for Brazil again, despite requests to return for the 1974 World Cup.

Pelé had played 92 matches for Brazil by the count most widely used, scoring 77 goals. With him in the team, Brazil had won 67, drawn 14 and lost 11.

He was 30 years old.

nodes.name: Santos 2–0 Ponte Preta
nodes.headline: Pelé's last official match for Santos, at Vila Belmiro, where he knelt on the pitch to say goodbye to the crowd.
nodes.story:
After 18 seasons, Pelé played his last official match for Santos against Ponte Preta at Vila Belmiro on 2 October 1974, in the Campeonato Paulista.

About 20 minutes into the first half he stopped, knelt on the pitch with his arms open to salute the crowd of about 20,000, and left the field.

Santos won 2–0. He would still play occasional friendlies for the club, but this was the end of his career in Brazilian club football.

He had scored 643 goals for Santos in official competitions, then the most by any player for a single club. Lionel Messi passed that record for Barcelona in December 2020. Within a year Pelé was playing again, in New York.

He was 33.

nodes.name: New York Cosmos 2–2 Dallas Tornado
nodes.headline: Pelé's first match for the New York Cosmos, broadcast to 22 countries, in which he scored.
nodes.story:
Pelé signed for the Cosmos on 10 June 1975. Five days later he played his first game for them, an exhibition against the Dallas Tornado at Downing Stadium on Randalls Island.

The match was shown on CBS and in 22 countries, and more than 300 journalists attended. The pitch was so bare that the groundsman reportedly sprayed it green for the cameras.

The match finished 2–2, and Pelé scored one of the Cosmos goals. The crowd was 22,278.

He had signed five days earlier for a reported $1.4 million a year and been presented at New York's 21 Club. The Cosmos finished third that season, too low to reach the play-offs, but crowds and coverage grew wherever he played.

He was 34.

nodes.name: New York Cosmos 2–1 Seattle Sounders
nodes.headline: The 1977 NASL final, won by the Cosmos: the last competitive match of Pelé's career.
nodes.story:
Soccer Bowl '77 was played at Civic Stadium in Portland, Oregon, on 28 August 1977. Steve Hunt put the Cosmos ahead in the 20th minute, and Tommy Ord equalised four minutes later. Giorgio Chinaglia scored the winner in the 78th minute.

Pelé did not score, but the 2–1 win gave the Cosmos their second NASL title. Franz Beckenbauer and Carlos Alberto played alongside him.

It was the last competitive match of his career. The crowd was 35,548.

Hunt was named the match's most valuable player. The game was broadcast on the TVS network. The Cosmos were coached by Eddie Firmani, who had taken over halfway through the season.

Pelé was 36. By Wikipedia's count he scored 17 goals in league and play-off games that season.

nodes.name: New York Cosmos 2–1 Santos
nodes.headline: Pelé's farewell match at Giants Stadium, in which he played one half for the Cosmos and one for Santos.
nodes.story:
Pelé's last match was an exhibition between his two clubs at Giants Stadium on 1 October 1977, before a sold-out crowd of 75,646. It was shown on ABC's *Wide World of Sports*. His father and wife were there, as were Muhammad Ali and Bobby Moore.

He played the first half for the Cosmos and scored with a free kick, the last goal of his career. At half-time the Cosmos retired his number 10 shirt. He played the second half for Santos.

The Cosmos won 2–1. It rained in the second half, and a Brazilian newspaper headline the next day said that even the sky was crying.

The Cosmos' winning goal was scored by Ramon Mifflin, who replaced Pelé for the second half. The captains of five World Cup-winning sides took part in the ceremony: Bellini, Mauro, Bobby Moore, Carlos Alberto and Franz Beckenbauer.

nodes.name: His first senior goal
nodes.headline: The first goal of Pelé's senior career, scored for Santos at 15 in a friendly against Corinthians de Santo André.
nodes.story:
Pelé scored in his first match for Santos, a 7–1 friendly win in Santo André on 7 September 1956. The goalkeeper, Zaluar, later joked about being the first of more than a thousand.

He had signed for Santos only that June and would not become a regular in the team until the following season.

nodes.name: His first World Cup goal
nodes.headline: The only goal of the 1958 quarter-final against Wales, which made Pelé the youngest World Cup scorer to that date.
nodes.story:
In the 66th minute of the quarter-final in Gothenburg, Pelé turned in the box and shot past the Welsh defence. He was 17 years and 239 days old.

It was the only goal of the match and took Brazil into the semi-finals against France.

nodes.name: The volley in the 1958 final
nodes.headline: Pelé's first goal in the 1958 final: he lifted the ball over a defender and volleyed it in, at 17.
nodes.story: Ten minutes after half-time, with Brazil 2–1 up, Pelé gathered the ball in the Swedish penalty area. He flicked it over the head of a defender and volleyed it past goalkeeper Kalle Svensson before it touched the ground. It is regularly listed among the best goals in World Cup history.
nodes.how: Flick over a defender, then a volley

nodes.name: The header that closed the 1958 final
nodes.headline: Pelé's second goal in the 1958 final, a header in the last minute that made the score 5–2.
nodes.story:
In the last minute of the final, Pelé headed in the fifth goal to make it 5–2. Moments later the match ended and he collapsed on the pitch.

It was his sixth goal of the tournament. Only Just Fontaine of France, with 13, scored more.

nodes.name: The gol de placa
nodes.headline: Pelé's solo goal against Fluminense at the Maracanã in 1961, which gave Brazil the phrase gol de placa.
nodes.story:
Near the end of the first half against Fluminense, Pelé took the ball in his own half and ran at the defence. He beat several players with changes of pace and feints, then beat goalkeeper Castilho.

A bronze plaque was put up at the Maracanã to mark it. Accounts differ on who paid for it: some credit the journalist Joelmir Beting, others the journalist Mário Filho. Since then Brazilians have called any exceptional goal a *gol de placa*.
nodes.how: Solo run from his own half

nodes.name: The 1,000th goal
nodes.headline: The penalty against Vasco da Gama at the Maracanã on 19 November 1969 counted as Pelé's 1,000th goal.
nodes.story:
Late in the second half against Vasco da Gama, Santos were given a penalty. Pelé took it and beat the Argentine goalkeeper Edgardo Andrada, who got a touch to the ball. Fans and reporters ran onto the pitch.

He dedicated the goal to the children of Brazil, asking people to think of poor children. Brazil's post office issued a stamp to mark it.

The count was disputed even then. It included friendlies, tour games and matches for military and state teams. Counting only official matches, his total at that point was much lower. The exact minute of the goal is given differently by different reports, so it is left out here.

nodes.name: The shot from his own half
nodes.headline: Pelé's attempt to lob the Czechoslovak goalkeeper from his own half in 1970, which went just wide.
nodes.story: Pelé noticed that Ivo Viktor, the Czechoslovak goalkeeper, was standing well off his line. He shot from just inside his own half. Viktor scrambled back, and the ball dropped just wide of the post. It did not go in, but it is one of the most replayed moments of the 1970 World Cup.
nodes.how: Long-range shot from his own half

nodes.name: The header Gordon Banks saved
nodes.headline: Pelé's header against England in 1970, stopped by Gordon Banks in what is often called the save of the century.
nodes.story:
Jairzinho crossed from the right and Pelé headed the ball down hard towards the corner. He was sure it was in. Banks dived across, got the fingers of his right hand to the ball after it bounced, and lifted it over the bar.

Pelé later said that of all the goals he had scored, the one people asked him about most was this one that he had not. The two became friends.

nodes.name: The dummy on Mazurkiewicz
nodes.headline: Pelé's run around Uruguay's goalkeeper in the 1970 semi-final, without touching the ball, which ended with a shot just wide.
nodes.story: Tostão passed into space and goalkeeper Ladislao Mazurkiewicz rushed out. Pelé got there first but did not touch the ball. He let it run past the keeper on one side while he went round the other. He caught up with it and shot on the turn, but it rolled just wide of the far post. The move is known in English as the Pelé runaround.

nodes.name: The header in the 1970 final
nodes.headline: Pelé's header that opened the scoring in the 1970 final, Brazil's 100th World Cup goal.
nodes.story:
In the 18th minute Rivellino crossed from the left. Pelé jumped and headed it in. He then leapt into Jairzinho's arms, a photograph that became one of the best-known images of the tournament.

The goal was Brazil's 100th at World Cups. Italy equalised before half-time, but Brazil scored three more in the second half.

nodes.name: The last goal of his career
nodes.headline: The free kick Pelé scored for the Cosmos against Santos in his farewell match, the last goal of his career.
nodes.story: In the first half of his farewell match, playing for the Cosmos, Pelé scored with a free kick from about 30 yards. It was the last goal of a career that, by the widest counts, had produced well over a thousand.

nodes.name: Pelé
nodes.headline: Edson Arantes do Nascimento (1940–2022), the Brazilian forward who won three World Cups, widely ranked the greatest of all time.
nodes.story:
Pelé was born Edson Arantes do Nascimento on 23 October 1940 in Três Corações, in Minas Gerais, and grew up poor in Bauru, in São Paulo state. His father, Dondinho, was a footballer whose career was cut short by a knee injury, and taught him the game. Where the nickname "Pelé" came from is not known for certain; he himself thought it began with his mispronouncing the name of a goalkeeper called Bilé.

He joined Santos in 1956, at 15, and made his debut for Brazil at 16. At 17 he scored twice in the 1958 World Cup final in Sweden. He went on to win the World Cup again in 1962, though injured early in the tournament, and in 1970 in Mexico, as the leader of a team often called the best in history. He is the only player to have won three.

He played as a forward, usually as a striker or inside forward, and later as a playmaker behind the strikers. He could shoot with either foot, was strong in the air and was known for his vision and passing as well as his goals. He stood 1.73 m tall.

With Santos he won two Copa Libertadores and two Intercontinental Cups. Brazil's government declared him a national treasure in 1961 to stop him being sold abroad, and he never played for a European club. After leaving Santos in 1974 he played three seasons for the New York Cosmos, winning the North American title in 1977 before retiring.

How many goals he scored is disputed. He and Guinness World Records counted more than 1,280, including friendlies and exhibitions. Counting only official matches, statisticians give figures between about 757 and 775.

After football he worked as a global ambassador for the sport, appeared in films, served with UN agencies and was Brazil's first Minister of Sport from 1995 to 1998. He shared FIFA's Player of the Century award with Diego Maradona in 2000 and was the IOC's Athlete of the Century in 1999.

He married three times and had seven children. He died in São Paulo on 29 December 2022, aged 82, of complications of colon cancer, and is buried in Santos.
