nodes.name: Dondinho
nodes.headline: João Ramos do Nascimento (1917–1996), Pelé's father, a centre forward who taught him to play.
nodes.story: Dondinho was a centre forward from Minas Gerais who played for several clubs, among them Atlético Mineiro, and was known for scoring with his head. A serious knee injury limited his career. He was Pelé's first coach and mentor, and Pelé named him as the person who taught him the game. He attended his son's farewell match in New York in 1977.

nodes.name: Celeste Arantes
nodes.headline: Celeste Arantes (1922–2024), known as Dona Celeste, Pelé's mother, who outlived him by nearly two years.
nodes.story: Celeste Arantes was born in Três Corações and married Dondinho there. They had three children: Edson (Pelé), Jair (Zoca) and Maria Lúcia. She did not want her sons to become footballers, because she knew how unsettled the life was. She was 100 when Pelé died and died herself in June 2024, aged 101.

nodes.name: Zoca
nodes.headline: Jair Arantes do Nascimento (1942–2020), Pelé's younger brother, who also played for Santos.
nodes.story:
Zoca was Pelé's younger brother and the son of Dondinho and Celeste. Like Pelé he played as a forward and spent part of his career at Santos, and he later worked as a coach.

His full name was Jair Arantes do Nascimento. He died in 2020.

nodes.name: Waldemar de Brito
nodes.headline: Waldemar de Brito (1913–1979), the former Brazil forward who coached Pelé in Bauru and took him to Santos in 1956.
nodes.story: Waldemar de Brito was a forward who played for clubs in Brazil and Argentina and for Brazil, and was among the best dribblers in the country in the 1930s. As coach of the Bauru Atlético Clube juniors he saw Pelé's talent. In 1956 he took the 15-year-old to Santos for a trial and, by Wikipedia's account, told the club's directors that the boy would be the best player in the world.

nodes.name: Vicente Feola
nodes.headline: Vicente Feola (1909–1975), the coach who picked a 17-year-old Pelé and led Brazil to its first World Cup in 1958.
nodes.story: Vicente Feola was a São Paulo coach who led Brazil at the 1958 World Cup. He brought Pelé into the team for the third match against the Soviet Union, against the advice of the team psychologist, and Brazil won the tournament. He returned as coach for the 1966 World Cup, where Brazil went out in the first round.

nodes.name: Mário Zagallo
nodes.headline: Mário Zagallo (1931–2024), Pelé's teammate at the 1958 and 1962 World Cups and Brazil's coach when they won in 1970.
nodes.story: Zagallo was a left winger who scored in the 1958 final and played in the 1962 one. As coach in 1970 he built the attacking team around Pelé, Jairzinho, Gérson, Tostão and Rivellino that won in Mexico. He was the first person to win the World Cup as both a player and a manager, and he won four World Cups in all, counting 1994 as assistant coach.

nodes.name: Garrincha
nodes.headline: Garrincha (1933–1983), Brazil's right winger and dribbler, who won the 1958 and 1962 World Cups alongside Pelé.
nodes.story: Manuel Francisco dos Santos, known as Garrincha, was a right winger famous for his dribbling. He and Pelé both made their World Cup debuts against the Soviet Union in 1958. When Pelé was injured in 1962, Garrincha led Brazil to the title and was the tournament's best player and joint top scorer. Brazil never lost a match in which both of them played.
nodes.photoCredit: Pressens Bild, public domain (PD-Chile), via Wikimedia Commons: https://commons.wikimedia.org/wiki/File:Garrincha_1962.jpg

nodes.name: Didi
nodes.headline: Didi (1928–2001), the midfielder who ran Brazil's play at the 1958 and 1962 World Cups and was named best player in 1958.
nodes.story: Waldyr Pereira, known as Didi, was a midfielder known for his passing and for the dipping free kick called the *folha seca*, or dry leaf. He played in three World Cups and won two, in 1958 and 1962. He was named the best player of the 1958 tournament, and he scored in the semi-final against France.

nodes.name: Vavá
nodes.headline: Vavá (1934–2002), Brazil's centre forward, who scored twice in the 1958 World Cup final.
nodes.story: Edvaldo Izídio Neto, known as Vavá, was a strong centre forward nicknamed "Steel Chest". He scored five goals at the 1958 World Cup, including two in the final, and four in 1962, when he was joint top scorer. He played for Vasco da Gama, Atlético Madrid and Palmeiras.

nodes.name: Nílton Santos
nodes.headline: Nílton Santos (1925–2013), Brazil's attacking left-back in the World Cup wins of 1958 and 1962.
nodes.story: Nílton Santos played his whole club career for Botafogo and was one of the first full-backs to attack down the wing. He won the World Cup with Pelé in 1958 and 1962. He was nicknamed *A Enciclopédia*, the Encyclopedia, for his knowledge of the game, and was named in the World Team of the 20th Century.

nodes.name: Coutinho
nodes.headline: Coutinho (1943–2019), the Santos centre forward who formed one of football's best-known partnerships with Pelé.
nodes.story: Antônio Wilson Vieira Honório, known as Coutinho, played alongside Pelé at Santos in the 1960s. The two were famous for their quick one-twos. Coutinho scored in both legs of the 1962 Intercontinental Cup and in the 1963 Libertadores final, and he was in Brazil's 1962 World Cup squad. He is credited with 368 goals in 457 matches.

nodes.name: Carlos Alberto Torres
nodes.headline: Carlos Alberto Torres (1944–2016), Brazil's captain in 1970, who scored the final goal of the final from Pelé's pass.
nodes.story: Carlos Alberto was an attacking right-back and Brazil's captain at the 1970 World Cup. He scored the fourth goal in the final against Italy, finishing a move with a shot from Pelé's pass. He joined Pelé at Santos in 1966 and played with him again at the New York Cosmos in 1977, and he consoled him at the end of his farewell match.
nodes.photoCredit: Richard Drew, public domain (PD-US-no notice), via Wikimedia Commons: https://commons.wikimedia.org/wiki/File:Carlos_Alberto_comforts_Pel%C3%A9_at_his_final_game_1977.jpg

nodes.name: Jairzinho
nodes.headline: Jairzinho (born 1944), Brazil's right winger in 1970, who scored in every match of the tournament.
nodes.story: Jair Ventura Filho, known as Jairzinho, was a fast and powerful right winger nicknamed the Hurricane. He was Brazil's leading scorer at the 1970 World Cup and scored in all six of their matches. His cross led to Gordon Banks's save from Pelé, and he scored the winner in that game.

nodes.name: Tostão
nodes.headline: Tostão (born 1947), the forward who partnered Pelé in Brazil's attack at the 1970 World Cup.
nodes.story: Eduardo Gonçalves de Andrade, known as Tostão, was a left-footed forward who played most of his career for Cruzeiro. He formed a strong partnership with Pelé in the 1970 team and started the move for Carlos Alberto's goal in the final. A detached retina, after he was hit in the face by the ball, ended his career early. He became a doctor and later a journalist and television pundit.

nodes.name: Rivellino
nodes.headline: Rivellino (born 1946), the attacking midfielder whose cross Pelé headed in to open the 1970 final.
nodes.story: Roberto Rivellino was an attacking midfielder known for his left-footed shooting and free kicks. At the 1970 World Cup he scored three goals, and he supplied the cross for Pelé's header in the final. He also scored in Pelé's last match for Brazil, against Yugoslavia in 1971.

nodes.name: Gordon Banks
nodes.headline: Gordon Banks (1937–2019), England's World Cup-winning goalkeeper, who made the famous save from Pelé's header in 1970.
nodes.story: Gordon Banks kept goal for England when they won the 1966 World Cup. In Guadalajara in 1970 he dived across his goal to push Pelé's downward header over the bar, a save often called the greatest ever made. Banks said people would remember him for that save more than for winning the World Cup. He and Pelé became friends, and Pelé unveiled a statue of him at Stoke in 2008.

nodes.name: Bobby Moore
nodes.headline: Bobby Moore (1941–1993), England's 1966 World Cup-winning captain, whom Pelé named the best defender he ever faced.
nodes.story: Bobby Moore captained West Ham United and England, and lifted the World Cup in 1966. Pelé called him the greatest defender he had played against. After Brazil beat England in 1970, the two swapped shirts and embraced in a photograph often used as an image of sportsmanship. Moore attended Pelé's farewell match in 1977.

nodes.name: Eusébio
nodes.headline: Eusébio (1942–2014), Benfica and Portugal's great forward, who faced Pelé in 1962 and knocked Brazil out in 1966.
nodes.story: Eusébio da Silva Ferreira, born in Mozambique, was Benfica's greatest scorer and the top scorer of the 1966 World Cup with nine goals. He played against Pelé in both legs of the 1962 Intercontinental Cup and scored twice when Portugal beat Brazil 3–1 in 1966. Like Pelé, he was called the Black Pearl and *o Rei*.

nodes.name: Franz Beckenbauer
nodes.headline: Franz Beckenbauer (1945–2024), West Germany's captain and sweeper, who joined Pelé at the Cosmos in 1977.
nodes.story: Franz Beckenbauer, nicknamed *der Kaiser*, captained West Germany to the 1974 World Cup and later won it as coach in 1990. He joined the New York Cosmos in 1977 and played alongside Pelé in the Soccer Bowl win that season.

nodes.name: Giorgio Chinaglia
nodes.headline: Giorgio Chinaglia (1947–2012), the Italian striker who partnered Pelé at the Cosmos and scored the winner in Soccer Bowl '77.
nodes.story: Giorgio Chinaglia grew up in Wales and led Lazio to the Italian title in 1974. He joined the New York Cosmos in 1976 and was paired with Pelé in attack. He scored the winning goal in Soccer Bowl '77, Pelé's last competitive match, and retired as the NASL's all-time top scorer.

nodes.name: Ladislao Mazurkiewicz
nodes.headline: Ladislao Mazurkiewicz (1945–2013), Uruguay's goalkeeper, beaten by Pelé's dummy in the 1970 semi-final but not by his shot.
nodes.story: Ladislao Mazurkiewicz kept goal for Uruguay from 1965 to 1974 and was named the best goalkeeper of the 1970 World Cup. In the semi-final against Brazil, Pelé went round him without touching the ball, but the shot that followed went wide. He also played for Atlético Mineiro in Brazil.

nodes.name: Rosemeri dos Reis Cholbi
nodes.headline: Pelé's first wife, married from 1966 to 1982 and mother of three of his children.
nodes.story:
Pelé married Rosemeri dos Reis Cholbi in 1966. They had three children: Kely Cristina, Edson (Edinho) and Jennifer. They divorced in 1982.

Their son Edinho later played in goal for Santos.

Their marriage lasted sixteen years. She attended his farewell match in New York in 1977.

nodes.name: Assíria Lemos Seixas
nodes.headline: Pelé's second wife, a psychologist and gospel singer, married from 1994 to 2008.
nodes.story:
Assíria Lemos Seixas is a psychologist and gospel singer. She married Pelé in 1994, and they had twins, Joshua and Celeste. They divorced in 2008.

Their twins were born in 1996 after fertility treatment. Joshua later played football in Santos's youth teams.

nodes.name: Marcia Aoki
nodes.headline: Pelé's third wife, married in 2016 and with him until his death in 2022.
nodes.story: Marcia Aoki, a Japanese-Brazilian businesswoman from Penápolis in São Paulo state, began a relationship with Pelé in 2010. They married in 2016, and she was with him in his last years. She attended his public wake in Santos in January 2023.

nodes.name: Edinho
nodes.headline: Edinho (born 1970), Pelé's son, a former Santos goalkeeper and later a coach.
nodes.story: Edson Cholbi do Nascimento, known as Edinho, is the son of Pelé and Rosemeri dos Reis Cholbi. He played in goal for Santos and other clubs until 1999, and later coached, including spells on the Santos staff. He spoke publicly about his father's health in his last years and attended his wake.

nodes.name: Childhood in Três Corações and Bauru
nodes.headline: Edson Arantes do Nascimento grew up poor in Bauru, learning football from his father with a ball made of rags.
nodes.story:
Edson Arantes do Nascimento was born on 23 October 1940 in Três Corações, a town in the south of Minas Gerais. His father, João Ramos do Nascimento, known as Dondinho, was a centre forward. His mother, Celeste Arantes, was from the same town. His parents named him after the American inventor Thomas Edison, dropping the "i". His birth certificate spelled it "Edison", and gave his birth date as 21 October, which he said was a mistake.

His family called him Dico. The name "Pelé" came later, at school, and nobody is quite sure why. Pelé said he probably got it after mispronouncing the name of Bilé, a goalkeeper he admired at Vasco da Gama. In his autobiography he said that neither he nor his school friends knew what the word meant.

Dondinho's career was held back by a serious knee injury. The family settled in Bauru, in the interior of São Paulo state, where they lived in poverty. As a boy Pelé worked as a server in tea shops to bring in money. He could not afford a proper ball, so he played with a sock stuffed with newspaper, or with a grapefruit. Dondinho taught him to play. His mother, who knew how hard a footballer's life could be, did not want him to make a career of it.

He played for small local teams with names such as Sete de Setembro and Ameriquinha. He also played futsal, the indoor five-a-side game, which was new in Bauru. He later said it taught him to think quickly in tight spaces, and it let him play against adults when he was about 14.

His most important team was the junior side of Bauru Atlético Clube. Its coach was Waldemar de Brito, a former Brazil forward. Under him, the juniors won two São Paulo state youth titles. In 1956 de Brito decided that the 15-year-old was ready for something bigger, and took him to the coast, to Santos.

nodes.name: Santos: discovery and debut (1956–1957)
nodes.headline: At 15 Pelé joined Santos, scored on his debut, and within a year was the top scorer in São Paulo and playing for Brazil.
nodes.story:
In 1956 Waldemar de Brito brought Pelé to Santos, an industrial port near the city of São Paulo, for a trial with Santos FC. By Wikipedia's account he told the club's directors that the boy would be the greatest player in the world. The coach, Luis Alonso Pérez, known as Lula, watched him train at Vila Belmiro and was impressed. Pelé signed a professional contract in June 1956.

He made his first-team debut on 7 September 1956, a public holiday in Brazil, in a friendly against Corinthians de Santo André. He scored once in a 7–1 win. It was the first goal of his senior career. The goalkeeper he beat, Zaluar, later made a small joke of it on his business card.

Santos were already state champions. When the 1957 season began, Pelé was in the starting team. At 16 he finished as the top scorer in the Campeonato Paulista, the São Paulo state league and one of the strongest competitions in Brazil.

Ten months after signing as a professional, he was called up to the national team. On 7 July 1957, aged 16, he played his first match for Brazil, against Argentina at the Maracanã in the Roca Cup. Brazil lost 2–1, but he scored. He remains the youngest player ever to score for Brazil. Three days later he scored again as Brazil won the return match in São Paulo and the trophy.

The following year he helped Santos win the 1958 Campeonato Paulista, his first major title with the club. He scored 58 goals in that season's championship, a record that still stands. By then Brazil's coach, Vicente Feola, had named him in the squad for the World Cup in Sweden.

nodes.name: Sweden 1958
nodes.headline: A 17-year-old Pelé scored six goals, including two in the final, as Brazil won the World Cup for the first time.
nodes.story:
Pelé arrived in Sweden in June 1958 with a knee injury. He was 17 and the youngest player in the tournament. He missed Brazil's first two matches: a 3–0 win over Austria and a 0–0 draw with England.

Before the third match, against the Soviet Union, the squad's psychologist told coach Vicente Feola that Pelé was too immature to play. Feola picked him anyway, along with the winger Garrincha. In Gothenburg on 15 June, Brazil won 2–0. Vavá scored both goals, the second from Pelé's pass.

Four days later, in the quarter-final against Wales, Pelé scored the only goal. He was then the youngest player ever to score at a World Cup. In the semi-final against France in Solna, with Brazil leading 2–1, he scored three times in the second half. Brazil won 5–2.

The final against the hosts, Sweden, was played at the Råsunda Stadium on 29 June. Sweden scored first. Vavá scored twice to turn the match round. Then Pelé scored a goal that is still shown on lists of the best in World Cup history. He brought the ball under control in the area, lifted it over a defender and volleyed it in. Zagallo made it 4–1, Sweden pulled one back, and in the last minute Pelé headed the fifth.

When the final whistle went, Pelé fainted on the pitch. He then cried on the shoulder of the goalkeeper, Gilmar, in a photograph published around the world. He had scored six goals in four matches and was named best young player of the tournament. Brazil became the first country to win a World Cup outside its own continent.

The tournament is also where he began wearing the number 10. The usual account is that Brazil's federation sent its squad list without shirt numbers, and FIFA assigned the numbers itself, giving Pelé the 10 more or less by chance. Back home, newspapers began calling him *O Rei*, the King. European clubs including Real Madrid and Juventus tried to sign him, without success.
nodes.photoCredit: Aftonbladet, public domain (PD-Sweden-photo), via Wikimedia Commons: https://commons.wikimedia.org/wiki/File:1958_VM-final_Sverige-Brasilien.jpg

nodes.name: The peak years at Santos (1959–1965)
nodes.headline: With Pelé at his peak, Santos became club champions of South America and of the world, twice each.
nodes.story:
Between 1959 and 1965 Pelé was at the height of his powers, and Santos built one of the most admired teams in football around him. Its players included Gilmar, Mauro, Zito, Dorval, Mengálvio, Coutinho, Pepe and Pelé, coached by Lula. Brazilians later called the side *Os Santásticos*.

In March 1959 Pelé was the top scorer at the South American Championship in Buenos Aires, with eight goals, and was named its best player. At home, Santos won the Campeonato Paulista in 1960, 1961, 1962, 1964 and 1965. From 1961 to 1965 they also won five national championships in a row, then called the Taça Brasil. Pelé was the top scorer in the state league every year from 1957 to 1965.

On 5 March 1961, against Fluminense at the Maracanã, he scored the solo goal that became known as the *gol de placa*. That year, President Jânio Quadros's government declared him an official national treasure, to stop foreign clubs buying him.

The Taça Brasil title took Santos into the Copa Libertadores, South America's club championship. They won it in 1962, beating Peñarol 3–0 in a play-off in Buenos Aires with two goals from Pelé. In the Intercontinental Cup that autumn they beat Benfica 3–2 in Rio and 5–2 in Lisbon. Pelé scored five goals in the two matches, including a hat-trick at the Estádio da Luz.

In 1963 Santos won the Libertadores again, beating Boca Juniors in both legs of the final; Pelé scored the winner in Buenos Aires. They then beat AC Milan in a three-match Intercontinental Cup, though Pelé missed the last two games. In November 1964 he scored eight goals in one league match, an 11–0 win over Botafogo of Ribeirão Preto at Vila Belmiro.

Santos earned large fees by touring the world, playing friendlies in Europe, Africa and Asia because crowds wanted to see Pelé. Those games make up much of his famous goal totals, and explain why counts differ so much. At this time he was, for a period, the highest-paid athlete in the world.
nodes.photoCredit: El Gráfico (photographer unknown), public domain (PD-AR-Photo), via Wikimedia Commons: https://commons.wikimedia.org/wiki/File:PEL%C3%89_-_1963.jpg

nodes.name: Chile 1962: the injury
nodes.headline: Pelé went to Chile as the world's best player but was injured in the second match; Brazil won the World Cup without him.
nodes.story:
By 1962 Pelé was 21 and widely considered the best player in the world. Brazil arrived in Chile as holders, with much of the 1958 team still together: Gilmar, Djalma Santos, Nílton Santos, Zito, Didi, Garrincha, Vavá and Zagallo. The coach was Aymoré Moreira.

Brazil's first match was against Mexico in Viña del Mar on 30 May. The first half was goalless. In the 56th minute Pelé set up Zagallo, and in the 73rd he scored the second goal himself. Brazil won 2–0.

Three days later they played Czechoslovakia at the same ground. Pelé was injured while shooting from distance. Substitutes were not allowed, so he stayed on the field, barely able to take part. The match ended 0–0. The injury kept him out for the rest of the tournament.

Without him, Garrincha carried the team. He scored twice in the quarter-final against England and starred in the 4–2 semi-final win over Chile, though he was sent off in it. He was named the best player of the tournament. Amarildo, from Botafogo, took Pelé's place and scored twice against Spain in the last group match. In the final in Santiago on 17 June, Brazil came from behind to beat Czechoslovakia 3–1.

Brazil had become the second country, after Italy, to win two World Cups in a row. For Pelé the tournament was bittersweet. Under the rules of the time, only players who played in the final received a winner's medal, so he did not get one. FIFA changed that rule in 1978 to include whole squads, and in 2007 Pelé was finally presented with a medal for 1962.

He returned to the Brazil team the following spring. In the 1963 Roca Cup against Argentina he scored a hat-trick, and on a European tour that year he scored three more against France in Paris.

nodes.name: England 1966
nodes.headline: Fouled out of two of Brazil's three matches, Pelé saw the holders go out in the first round and vowed never to play another World Cup.
nodes.story:
Brazil went to England in 1966 as two-time holders, with Vicente Feola back as coach. The squad still included Garrincha, Djalma Santos and Gilmar from earlier wins, alongside younger players such as Jairzinho, Tostão and Gérson. Their three group matches were all at Goodison Park in Liverpool.

The first, against Bulgaria on 12 July, was won 2–0. Pelé scored the first goal and Garrincha the second. Pelé became the first player to score at three World Cups in a row. But the Bulgarian defenders kicked him repeatedly, and he left the match with a knee injury.

He missed the second match, against Hungary. Brazil lost 3–1, their first World Cup defeat in twelve years. Brazil had never lost a match in which both Pelé and Garrincha played.

For the last game, against Portugal on 19 July, Pelé was brought back though not fully fit. Brazil had to win. Portugal, with Eusébio, led 2–0 within half an hour. The defender João Morais fouled Pelé twice, and the referee, George McCabe, did not send him off. That decision is often listed among the worst refereeing errors in World Cup history. Substitutions were not allowed, so Pelé could do little more than limp; accounts differ on whether he stayed on until the end. Brazil lost 3–1.

The holders were out in the first round. The tournament was remembered for its rough play, and Pelé was its most obvious victim. Afterwards he said he would never play in a World Cup again.

He kept that promise for three years. In 1969 he agreed to return to the national team, which had a new coach, João Saldanha, and a new generation of players. The road to Mexico had begun.

nodes.name: The 1,000th goal (1969)
nodes.headline: On 19 November 1969 Pelé scored his 1,000th goal by the count of the time, a penalty at the Maracanã that stopped the country.
nodes.story:
By the late 1960s Pelé's goal count was followed in Brazil the way other countries follow an election. The tally kept by Santos and the press included every goal: league and cup matches, but also friendlies, foreign tours, and games for military and state teams. In late 1969 it approached 1,000.

Santos played Vasco da Gama at the Maracanã in Rio de Janeiro on 19 November 1969, in the national championship. The score was 1–1 late in the second half when the referee gave Santos a penalty. Pelé took it. The Argentine goalkeeper, Edgardo Andrada, guessed the right way and touched the ball, but could not keep it out.

Photographers and fans poured onto the pitch. He was carried around the ground, and in the interviews that followed he dedicated the goal to the children of Brazil, asking people to think about poor children who needed food and clothes. The goal became known as *O Milésimo*, "the thousandth". Brazil's post office issued a commemorative stamp, and Santos won the match 2–1.

How many of those goals came in official matches is a different question. Statisticians who count only competitive games give him far fewer at that date, and his career total in official matches is put at between about 757 and 775. The milestone was real by the standard of its time, which counted friendlies freely. Accounts of the night also differ in details such as the minute of the goal and the size of the crowd.

The same year brought another story often told about Pelé. When Santos toured Nigeria in 1969, during the civil war, it is said that the two sides agreed a ceasefire of 48 hours so people could watch him play. Santos drew 2–2 with Stationery Stores in Lagos, with Pelé scoring both goals. But the story is disputed. One early source for it is a 1975 article in *Ebony* magazine. Local researchers have found no contemporary report of a ceasefire, some versions place the match in Benin City instead, and Pelé himself said he was not sure there had been one, only that security was very tight.
nodes.photoCredit: Correios do Brasil (Brazilian post office), public domain (PD-BrazilGov), via Wikimedia Commons: https://commons.wikimedia.org/wiki/File:Selo_Pel%C3%A9_1000_gols_10_cts.jpg

nodes.name: Mexico 1970
nodes.headline: In his fourth and last World Cup, Pelé led one of the finest teams ever assembled to Brazil's third title.
nodes.story:
When Brazil asked Pelé back in 1969 he first refused, then agreed. He scored six goals in six qualifying matches. By the finals the coach was Mário Zagallo, his teammate from 1958 and 1962. He picked an attacking side in which Jairzinho, Gérson, Tostão, Rivellino and Pelé all played together, with Carlos Alberto as captain.

Brazil played their group in Guadalajara. Against Czechoslovakia on 3 June they fell behind, then won 4–1. Pelé scored, becoming only the second man after Uwe Seeler to score at four World Cups. In the same game he tried to lob the goalkeeper from inside his own half, and the ball went just wide.

Four days later Brazil met England, the champions. Pelé met Jairzinho's cross with a downward header that Gordon Banks somehow pushed over the bar. Jairzinho scored the winner after Pelé laid the ball into his path. At the end Pelé and Bobby Moore swapped shirts and embraced. Pelé then scored twice in a 3–2 win over Romania.

Brazil beat Peru 4–2 in the quarter-final and Uruguay 3–1 in the semi-final. Against Uruguay Pelé did not score, but he produced his famous dummy, letting the ball run past goalkeeper Ladislao Mazurkiewicz on one side as he ran round the other, before shooting just wide.

The final against Italy was played at the Estadio Azteca in Mexico City on 21 June. In the 18th minute Pelé headed in Rivellino's cross and jumped into Jairzinho's arms. Italy equalised. In the second half Gérson scored, and Pelé headed a long free kick down for Jairzinho to make it 3–1. The last goal began deep in Brazil's half and ended with Pelé rolling the ball, without looking, into the path of Carlos Alberto, who struck it in.

Brazil won 4–1 and kept the Jules Rimet Trophy for good. Pelé had four goals and six assists, and was later named the player of the tournament. He remains the only footballer to win three World Cups.
nodes.photoCredit: Associated Press, via El Gráfico, public domain (PD-AR-Photo, PD-US-no notice), via Wikimedia Commons: https://commons.wikimedia.org/wiki/File:Pele_celebrating_1970.jpg

nodes.name: Leaving Brazil and Santos (1971–1974)
nodes.headline: Pelé said goodbye to the national team in 1971 and to Santos in 1974, and turned down a return for the 1974 World Cup.
nodes.story:
After Mexico, Pelé decided to stop playing for Brazil while he was still at the top. His last international goal came against Austria in São Paulo on 11 July 1971. A week later, on 18 July, he played his farewell match for the national team against Yugoslavia at the Maracanã. The game ended 2–2, in front of a very large crowd.

He finished with 77 goals in 92 matches by the count most used in English-language sources, a Brazilian record that lasted more than fifty years. The Brazilian federation's own count, which includes games against clubs, is 95 goals in 113 matches.

He kept playing for Santos. The great side of the early 1960s had broken up, but the club still won titles, and Pelé could still decide matches. In 1971 he turned down an offer from Paris Saint-Germain, then a young club in France. In 1973 Santos shared the Campeonato Paulista with Portuguesa, after the referee ended a penalty shoot-out early by mistake, and Pelé was the league's top scorer for the eleventh time. That year he was also named South American Footballer of the Year.

In December 1973 he played in a farewell match for Garrincha and scored for a Brazil team against a Rest of the World side.

As the 1974 World Cup in West Germany approached, he was asked to return to the national team. He said no. Brazil went to the tournament without him and finished fourth.

His last official match for Santos was against Ponte Preta at Vila Belmiro on 2 October 1974. About 20 minutes in, he stopped, knelt on the pitch and spread his arms to salute the crowd, then left the field. Santos won 2–0. He had played 18 seasons for the club. He was 33, and for a few months it looked as if his playing days were over.

nodes.name: New York Cosmos (1975–1977)
nodes.headline: Pelé came out of retirement to play for the New York Cosmos, drew huge crowds, and finished with the 1977 NASL title.
nodes.story:
The New York Cosmos had been trying to sign Pelé since the club was founded. In June 1975 he agreed. He signed on 10 June for a reported $1.4 million a year, a huge sum for an athlete at the time, and was presented to the press at New York's 21 Club in a chaotic scene.

Five days later he played his first game, an exhibition against the Dallas Tornado at Downing Stadium on Randalls Island. CBS broadcast it, and the match was shown in 22 countries. The pitch had so little grass that the groundsman reportedly sprayed it green. Pelé scored in a 2–2 draw.

Soccer in the United States was struggling. Matches drew small crowds and little coverage. Pelé changed that almost at once. Other famous players followed him to the North American Soccer League: Giorgio Chinaglia came to the Cosmos in 1976, and Franz Beckenbauer and Carlos Alberto in 1977. George Best, Johan Cruyff, Eusébio, Bobby Moore and Gordon Banks all played in the league in these years. Pelé was voted the league's most valuable player in 1976.

In 1977 the Cosmos moved to the new Giants Stadium in New Jersey. Crowds grew to more than 70,000. On 28 August, in Portland, Oregon, they beat the Seattle Sounders 2–1 to win Soccer Bowl '77. It was Pelé's last competitive match.

His farewell came on 1 October 1977 at Giants Stadium, against Santos, before 75,646 people. Muhammad Ali, Bobby Moore and Pelé's father were there. He played the first half for the Cosmos and scored with a free kick, then played the second half for Santos. The Cosmos retired his number 10. It rained, and a Brazilian newspaper wrote the next day that even the sky was crying.

Counting league and play-off games, he scored 37 goals in 64 matches for the Cosmos.

nodes.name: After football
nodes.headline: After retiring, Pelé acted, wrote, represented the UN and UNESCO, and served as Brazil's first Minister of Sport.
nodes.story:
After his farewell in 1977 Pelé became football's best-known ambassador. He travelled for sponsors and for the game, and remained one of the most recognised people in the world.

He also worked in films. He had already acted on Brazilian television, and in 1981 he starred with Sylvester Stallone and Michael Caine in *Escape to Victory*, John Huston's film about prisoners of war who play a match against a German team. He published several autobiographies, and he was the subject of documentaries including *Pelé Eterno* (2004) and the Netflix film *Pelé* (2021). The 2016 drama *Pelé: Birth of a Legend* told the story of his early life and the 1958 World Cup.

In 1992 the United Nations made him an ambassador for ecology and the environment, and he was later named a UNESCO Goodwill Ambassador. In January 1995 President Fernando Henrique Cardoso appointed him Brazil's first Minister of Sport. In office he proposed legislation to reduce corruption in Brazilian football, which became known as the Pelé Law. He left on 29 April 1998, when the ministry was abolished. In 1997 he received an honorary knighthood from Queen Elizabeth II at Buckingham Palace.

His business life was mixed. In 1993 he publicly accused the head of the Brazilian football federation, Ricardo Teixeira, of corruption, starting a long feud that led to his exclusion from the 1994 World Cup draw. In 2016 he sued Samsung in the United States over an advert that he said used a lookalike; the case was later settled.

The honours kept coming. The International Olympic Committee named him Athlete of the Century in 1999, and in 2000 he shared FIFA's Player of the Century award with Diego Maradona. In 2010 he became honorary president of a revived New York Cosmos, and in 2014 he received the first FIFA Ballon d'Or Prix d'Honneur. In 2018 he started the Pelé Foundation for children's education and poverty relief.

By then his health was declining. He had a hip operation in 2012, and from 2017 he often appeared in public in a wheelchair.

nodes.name: Illness, death and legacy
nodes.headline: Pelé died of colon cancer in December 2022 at 82; more than 230,000 people filed past his coffin in Santos.
nodes.story:
In September 2021, routine tests found a tumour in Pelé's colon. On 4 September he had surgery at the Albert Einstein Israelite Hospital in São Paulo, and he then began chemotherapy. He announced the operation himself on social media.

In early 2022 doctors found that the cancer had spread to his intestine, lungs and liver. He was admitted to the same hospital on 29 November with a respiratory infection after catching COVID-19. In early December it was reported that the cancer was no longer responding to chemotherapy and that he was receiving palliative care. Later that month the hospital said he needed more care for kidney and heart problems, and he could not go home for Christmas as his family had hoped.

Pelé died on 29 December 2022, aged 82. The cause was multiple organ failure as a complication of colon cancer. His mother, Celeste, then 100, survived him.

Brazil declared three days of national mourning. Flags were lowered at FIFA's headquarters in Zürich, and landmarks from Christ the Redeemer to Wembley Stadium were lit in his honour. On 2 January 2023 his coffin, draped in the flags of Brazil and Santos, was placed on the pitch at Vila Belmiro. More than 230,000 people filed past over two days, among them President Luiz Inácio Lula da Silva. On 3 January a procession carried him through the streets of Santos to the Memorial Necrópole Ecumênica, where he was buried.

His legacy reaches well beyond his statistics. The Guardian's Barney Ronay called him the first global sports superstar, and his emergence in 1958 made him one of the first Black global sporting stars. He linked football with the phrase "the beautiful game". In 2023 the Michaelis Portuguese dictionary added *pelé* as an adjective meaning exceptional or unique, after a campaign signed by more than 125,000 people, and Rwanda renamed its national stadium in Kigali in his honour. His goal record for Brazil stood until Neymar passed it in September 2023.

nodes.name: What was Pelé's real name?
nodes.answer: Pelé's real name was Edson Arantes do Nascimento. His parents named him after the inventor Thomas Edison, though his birth certificate spelled it "Edison". At home he was called Dico.

nodes.name: Why was he called Pelé?
nodes.answer: Nobody knows for certain. Pelé himself thought the nickname came from his childhood mispronunciation of Bilé, a goalkeeper at Vasco da Gama. He said that neither he nor his school friends knew what the word meant.

nodes.name: How many goals did Pelé score?
nodes.answer: It depends on what you count, and the figure is disputed. Counting friendlies and exhibitions, Guinness World Records credits him with 1,279 goals in 1,363 matches, FIFA uses 1,281, and Pelé himself claimed 1,283. Counting only official competitive matches, statisticians give between about 757 (the figure used by ESPN) and 775 (RSSSF, as cited by Wikipedia).

nodes.name: How many World Cups did Pelé win?
nodes.answer: Pelé won three World Cups, in 1958, 1962 and 1970, and is the only player to have done so. He played in four, also appearing in 1966, and scored 12 goals in 14 World Cup matches.

nodes.name: Which clubs did Pelé play for?
nodes.answer: Pelé played professionally for only two clubs: Santos in Brazil, from 1956 to 1974, and the New York Cosmos in the United States, from 1975 to 1977. As a boy he played for the junior team of Bauru Atlético Clube.

nodes.name: Did Pelé ever play in Europe?
nodes.answer: No, Pelé never played for a European club. Real Madrid, Juventus, Manchester United and Inter Milan all tried to sign him, and in 1961 Brazil's government declared him a national treasure to keep him at home. He did play many friendlies in Europe on tour with Santos and Brazil, and the 1958 and 1966 World Cups.

nodes.name: What shirt number did Pelé wear?
nodes.answer: Pelé wore the number 10, for Santos, Brazil and the Cosmos. He first wore it at the 1958 World Cup: by the usual account, Brazil's federation sent its squad list without numbers, and FIFA assigned them, giving the 10 to Pelé more or less by chance. The Cosmos retired the number for him in 1977.

nodes.name: When and how did Pelé die?
nodes.answer: Pelé died on 29 December 2022, aged 82, at the Albert Einstein Israelite Hospital in São Paulo. The cause was multiple organ failure as a complication of colon cancer, diagnosed in 2021. He is buried at the Memorial Necrópole Ecumênica in Santos.

nodes.name: How tall was Pelé?
nodes.answer: Pelé was about 1.73 m (5 ft 8 in) tall, the height given by Wikipedia. He was not big, but he was strong, fast and very good in the air.

nodes.name: What position did Pelé play?
nodes.answer: Pelé was a forward. Early on he played mostly as a striker, centre forward or inside forward, and later in his career he often played a deeper playmaking role behind the strikers, as an attacking midfielder.

nodes.name: Was Pelé FIFA's Player of the Century?
nodes.answer: Yes, jointly with Diego Maradona. In 2000 Maradona won FIFA's internet poll, while a committee of journalists, officials and coaches, together with FIFA Magazine readers, chose Pelé, so FIFA gave the award to both. Separately, the IOC named Pelé Athlete of the Century in 1999.

nodes.name: What was Pelé's best goal?
nodes.answer: There is no agreed answer. The best known are his volley in the 1958 World Cup final and the solo run against Fluminense in 1961 that gave Brazil the phrase gol de placa. Pelé himself said his most memorable goal was one against Juventus of São Paulo in August 1959, of which no film survives.

nodes.name: When did Pelé score his 1,000th goal?
nodes.answer: Pelé scored his 1,000th goal, by the count of the time, on 19 November 1969, from a penalty for Santos against Vasco da Gama at the Maracanã. The count included friendlies and exhibition matches; counting only official games, he had far fewer at that date.

nodes.name: What does "O Rei" mean?
nodes.answer: "O Rei" is Portuguese for "the King". The Brazilian press began calling Pelé that after the 1958 World Cup, and he was also known as *O Rei do Futebol*, the King of Football, and *A Pérola Negra*, the Black Pearl.

nodes.name: Did Pelé play in the United States?
nodes.answer: Yes. Pelé played for the New York Cosmos of the North American Soccer League from 1975 to 1977, winning the league's championship in 1977. His farewell match, against Santos, was played at Giants Stadium in New Jersey on 1 October 1977.

nodes.name: Was Pelé a government minister?
nodes.answer: Yes. Pelé was Brazil's first Minister of Sport, appointed by President Fernando Henrique Cardoso, from 1 January 1995 to 29 April 1998, when the ministry was abolished. He proposed the anti-corruption football legislation known as the Pelé Law.

nodes.name: How many matches and goals did Pelé play and score for Brazil?
nodes.answer: Pelé scored 77 goals in 92 matches for Brazil between 1957 and 1971, by the count most widely used. That total includes one 1968 match that FIFA does not recognise as official. The Brazilian Football Confederation, which also counts matches against club sides, credits him with 95 goals in 113 games.

nodes.name: Is Pelé the footballer connected to Pele the diagram tool?
nodes.answer: No. pele.wiki also covers Pele, an unrelated open-source library that renders Mermaid diagrams, at pele.wiki/. That project says it is named after the Hawaiian goddess of volcanoes and fire, not the footballer.
